strengths: Insightful KL-projection analysis of constrained decoding showing how cumulative 'projection tax' from low feasible mass causes distortion and trajectory bias
Context-dependent feasible mass insight (Eq. 10) elegantly motivates the approach—conditioning on draft increases probability of valid tokens without changing parameters
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 4 benchmarks, 6 model sizes (1B-14B), 3 baseline methods, multiple constraint types with consistent improvements
Substantial practical gains: +24pp on GSM8K (1B model), 253% parameter efficiency improvement on MATH500, demonstrates parameter-efficient model composition
Test-time scaling superior to constrained decoding baseline, better test-time allocation to semantic planning than syntactic refinement
Training-free method, reproducible with promised code release, extensive appendix with prompts/grammars/examples, clear algorithmic description
Well-presented: effective toy example (Figures 2-3), clear narrative from problem motivation to solution to experiments, intuitive figures
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core method (generate unconstrained then constrain) is straightforward application of feasible-mass insight; pattern exists in other domains
Missing critical ablation studies: no comparison of same-model vs. smaller-projector tradeoffs, no systematic analysis of draft quality impact, no empirical comparison of draft selection criteria
No statistical significance testing despite stochastic sampling nature: all results appear to be single runs without error bars or confidence intervals
Unfair experimental comparisons: two-model DCCD vs. single-model CD doesn't isolate method contribution; missing comparison to single-model CD with equivalent total parameter budget

Inconsistent results across tasks: GSM-Symbolic shows zero improvement in several cases (1B: 9.0%→9.0%, 1.5B: 23.0%→23.0%); FOLIO shows marginal absolute gains (~2pp) with very low baseline accuracies (0-31%), deserves investigation
Computational cost inadequately addressed: DCCD requires 2× forward passes doubling inference latency, but wall-clock time comparisons missing—critical for practical deployment
Weak baseline comparisons: Constrained Prompting and Few-Shot are basic; no comparison to other recent constrained decoding improvements (e.g., Banerjee et al. 2025 cited but not compared)

Theoretical gaps: connection between feasible mass increase and accuracy improvement relies on informal arguments and loose Pinsker's inequality bounds; no formal characterization of draft conditioning benefit

Method details underexplored: unclear why cumulative log feasible mass is optimal for draft selection vs. alternatives; limited guidance on when same-model vs. smaller-projector is preferred; best-of-K underexplored
Response confidence analysis (Figure 7) uses joint probability p_draft·p_proj which isn't directly comparable to constrained decoding in terms of what confidence means

strengths: Clear motivation with effective KL-projection analysis of constrained decoding's failure modes
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple scales (1B–14B), datasets, and baselines with consistent improvements (up to +24pp)
Simple, training-free, and practical two-step procedure easy to implement and deploy
Thorough reproducibility details in appendices with case studies and dataset specifications
Demonstrates parameter efficiency gains (253% on MATH500) and better test-time scaling than constrained decoding
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Two-step heuristic (draft then constrain) is intuitive but lacks innovation expected at ICML

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Identifies feasible mass as the problem but doesn't rigorously prove DCCD reduces total projection tax; missing formal characterization of when/why draft conditioning increases feasible mass
Unfair baseline comparison: DCCD uses 2× inference passes; no wall-clock time analysis or comparison with CD given 2× budget; claimed parameter efficiency with smaller projectors is unvalidated
Missing critical ablations: No comparison of K=1 vs K>1, projector size sensitivity, draft length effects, or alternative draft selection criteria
No statistical significance testing: Results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests across all benchmarks
Incomplete failure analysis: No discussion of when DCCD underperforms, when CD is preferable, or failure modes when drafts are semantically wrong
Questionable draft selection: Cumulative log feasible mass criterion (Algorithm 1, line 12) is arbitrary and not justified; alternative criteria mentioned but not explored

strengths: Clear problem identification with rigorous KL-projection analysis showing how low feasible mass α(h_t) causes cumulative distortion and trajectory bias

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 datasets, 6 models (1B-14B), and 3 constraint types, consistently outperforming constrained decoding baselines with particularly strong gains on GSM8K (15.2% → 39.0% for 1B model)
Practical parameter efficiency demonstrated: smaller 2-model compositions (e.g., 1.5B+1.5B) match or exceed much larger single-model CD baselines, enabling cost-effective deployment
Training-free approach with detailed reproducibility support including prompts, constraints, examples, and case studies in appendices

Superior test-time scaling: DCCD converts additional compute into larger gains than CD (Figure 6), suggesting allocating test-time budget to draft sampling is more effective than repeated constrained sampling
Well-motivated toy example (Figures 2-3) that effectively illustrates the feasible mass problem and how conditioning on a draft increases probability on structural tokens
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: once the feasible mass problem is identified, the solution (unconstrained draft followed by constrained decoding) is relatively straightforward; innovation is primarily in problem diagnosis rather than methodology

Critical missing analysis of computational cost: DCCD requires two forward passes, effectively doubling inference latency compared to single-pass CD; no wall-clock time comparisons provided despite being crucial for practical deployment

Insufficient justification of design choices: best-of-K selection uses cumulative log feasible mass (Eq. S^(k)) with no empirical comparison to mentioned alternatives (verifiers, judges, voting); no guidance on choosing p_proj size or whether it can always be smaller than p_draft

Incomplete failure mode and sensitivity analysis: no systematic study of how draft quality affects final performance, what happens when drafts are poor, or when DCCD might underperform; no ablations on selection criteria or model size choices

Weak experimental baselines and incomplete analysis: constrained prompting/few-shot are prompt-only methods not directly comparable to CD; significant variation in improvements across datasets (GSM8K +24pp vs. FOLIO +2-6pp) without explaining when method helps most; no error bars, significance testing, or inter-annotator agreement for LLM-as-judge evaluation

Missing practical guidance: despite noting larger gains for smaller models, paper doesn't explain why (lower feasible mass? KL sensitivity?) or provide decision criteria for practitioners to choose DCCD over alternatives
Limited scope and incremental nature: approach is specific to structured generation; core technique lacks novelty once motivated; improvements are meaningful but not transformative

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear KL-projection theoretical framing that elegantly explains constrained decoding's failure modes through the concept of 'projection tax' and feasible mass
Simple, training-free, and immediately deployable solution that requires no model modifications, making it highly practical for real-world LLM systems

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four datasets, six model scales (1B–14B), multiple constraint types, and diverse reasoning domains with consistent improvements (5–24 pts) and compelling parameter-efficiency gains (e.g., 1.5B+1.5B outperforms 14B baseline)

Rigorous transparency with extensive ablations: clean isolation of CD's harm (Table 3), draft quality analysis (Table 6), recovery rate decomposition (Table 9), feasible mass correlation (r=0.71), and budget-matched comparisons disproving 'more tokens' hypothesis

Exceptional breadth of analysis including non-verifiable tasks (78–80.5% win rates), test-time scaling behavior, schema tightness effects, and comparison with thinking-token approaches, with detailed case studies (Section J–K) demonstrating method effectiveness

Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 2–3) and well-structured toy example that intuitively communicates the mechanism; reproducibility enhanced through detailed prompts, constraints, and dataset examples in appendix
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: while the KL-projection view is clearly presented, the core insight that hard constraints distort model distributions is known; the analysis is more a useful quantification than a fundamentally new conceptual contribution

DCCD is fundamentally bounded by stage-1 draft quality (Table 6 shows draft accuracy as ceiling) with minimal error recovery (0.2–3.3%, Table 9), meaning the method primarily performs structured realization rather than semantic correction; this fundamental limitation deserves more prominent discussion upfront

Requires two inference passes introducing ~13% latency overhead (Table 5), creating a non-trivial practical cost in latency-sensitive deployments without clear guidance on when this tradeoff is worthwhile compared to alternatives like K-sampling with CD

Incomplete characterization of failure modes and constraint-type dependence: no systematic analysis of when DCCD underperforms, which constraint types trigger strongest projection tax, or guidance on applicability—practitioners must resort to trial-and-error

Draft selection via cumulative log feasible mass is pragmatic but underexplored: Table 11 shows majority voting outperforms it, undermining theoretical justification; no guidance on optimal K, and framework remains agnostic to alternative signals (verifiers, task-specific metrics)

Limited exploration of practical design choices: constraint-type generalizability (beyond JSON/grammar/FOL) unexplored, optimal sizing of draft vs. projector models not investigated, and FOLIO's lower improvements (31.53% on 7B) lack explanation, limiting practitioner guidance

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single-run results especially problematic for smaller datasets (FOLIO ~1k examples); variance assessment across model scales absent

Important results relegated to appendix (feasible mass correlation, thinking-token comparison, budget-matched ablations) weakening main narrative; non-verifiable task evaluation uses single-judge LLM-as-judge (Qwen-14B) with inherent unreliability concerns

strengths: Clear articulation of the projection tax problem with sound KL-divergence analysis (Section 3.1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (GSM8K, MATH500, GSM-Symbolic, FOLIO), model scales (1B-14B), and constraint types
Practical insight on parameter efficiency: smaller model pairs outperform larger single-model baselines under constrained decoding
Thorough appendix with extensive ablations (draft quality bounds, budget-matched comparisons, draft-length effects, schema tightness)
Effective presentation with clear visualizations (Figures 2-3) that communicate core ideas intuitively
Consistent improvements across benchmarks (+10-24 percentage points)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward conditioning (generate draft, then constrain); lacks principled insights or algorithmic innovation

Severe practical limitations inadequately addressed: DCCD requires ~36-50% higher inference latency (Table 5), making adoption prohibitive in production systems; this cost-benefit tradeoff is not properly analyzed against alternatives

Fundamental dependency on draft quality undermines claims: DCCD accuracy is capped by unconstrained draft accuracy; Table 6 shows Stage 2 preserves correctness 73-84% but recovers from errors only 0.2-3.3%, indicating the approach reformats rather than improves reasoning

Weak theoretical motivation for draft selection: Table 11 shows proposed feasible-mass selection underperforms majority voting for multi-draft selection, contradicting the paper's theoretical framework

Insufficient comparison with alternatives: missing comparisons with instruction tuning, verifier-based approaches, simpler two-stage methods, and speculative decoding; thinking-token comparison (Table 13) limited to one model
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; single-run evaluations; some datasets are small (FOLIO ~40 examples per split); improvements may be within noise

Limited scope of evaluation: experiments focus primarily on mathematical reasoning and logic; generalization to other structured generation tasks (code, entity extraction, etc.) unclear; FOLIO improvements are weak (2-7pp)
Reproducibility concerns: code not provided; implementation details missing (how is draft formatted when passed to Stage 2?); hyperparameter choices not justified

Overstated contributions: framed as 'training-free' but incurs 2× inference cost; 'artifact' claim about quality-validity tradeoff is not fully supported (Table 6 shows tradeoff is real, just managed differently)
Weak multi-draft selection criterion: feasible mass shows only moderate correlation (r=0.71) with accuracy; relationship may be circular rather than causal

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation through KL-projection analysis showing constrained decoding induces cumulative 'projection tax' via low feasible mass, with elegant toy examples and distributional stability justification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets (GSM8K, MATH500, GSM-Symbolic, FOLIO), 6 model scales (1B-14B), with strict joint evaluation of correctness and structural validity

Substantial and consistent empirical improvements: up to +24 percentage points (1B: 15.2→39.0% on GSM8K) with gains across all settings; parameter efficiency enables smaller model pairs to match 14B baselines

Valuable isolation analysis (Table 3) decomposing prompt vs. CD effects, showing CD itself causes 10-30pt degradation independent of prompting; extensive ablations (Tables 6-12) and mechanism analysis (Table 9)
Practical training-free approach preserving exact validity guarantees; agnostic to constraint type; easy to implement and deploy in existing systems
Superior test-time scaling: DCCD converts additional compute into larger gains than CD (78-83% vs 64-73% on GSM8K with n=13); excellent case studies demonstrating mechanism
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: focused on mathematical reasoning and logic; generalization to code generation, semantic parsing, data extraction tasks remains unclear; non-verifiable tasks experiment is narrow
Method fundamentally bounded by draft quality: Stage 2 rarely recovers from incorrect drafts (0.2-3.3%, Table 9); approach limited to settings where Stage 1 accuracy is already reasonable
Feasible mass scoring suboptimal for multi-draft selection: majority voting outperforms it (Table 11), suggesting the theoretical justification for this selection criterion may be weaker than claimed

Incomplete mechanism explanation: why conditioning on unconstrained draft specifically increases probability on schema-consistent tokens lacks principled theoretical justification beyond empirical observation
Modest latency overhead (~13% wall-clock increase) from two-stage inference; matters in latency-sensitive applications and limits single-pass deployment benefits
Missing failure mode analysis: no systematic study of when DCCD underperforms CD, adversarial cases, or out-of-domain degradation; feasible mass-correctness correlation is moderate (0.71)
Conceptually incremental: decomposing reasoning from formatting, while practical, follows intuitive intuition; gains diminish for larger models (14B: 47.6→58.6 on MATH500)
